claim: Intratracheal instillation of DT in transgenic mice expressing human diphtheria toxin (DT) receptor targeted to ECs resulted in ablation of >70% of lung ECs.
source: Intratracheal instillation of DT in transgenic mice expressing human diphtheria toxin (DT) receptor targeted to ECs resulted in ablation of >70% of lung ECs, producing severe ALI with near complete resolution by 7 days.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing ~70% reduction in EC numbers at 3 days post-DT administration (Figure 1D and E).

claim: DT-induced EC ablation produced severe ALI with near complete resolution by 7 days.
source: Intratracheal instillation of DT in transgenic mice expressing human diphtheria toxin (DT) receptor targeted to ECs resulted in ablation of >70% of lung ECs, producing severe ALI with near complete resolution by 7 days.
evidence: Supported by lung injury scoring, Evans blue permeability assays, and flow cytometry showing recovery of EC numbers by day 7 (Figures 1E, 2B, 2D).

claim: Eight distinct endothelial clusters were resolved using single-cell RNA sequencing.
source: Using single-cell RNA sequencing, eight distinct endothelial clusters were resolved, including alveolar aerocytes (aCap) ECs expressing apelin at baseline and general capillary (gCap) ECs expressing the apelin receptor.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq analysis and UMAP visualization showing 8 EC clusters (Figure 4A).

claim: Alveolar aerocytes (aCap) ECs express apelin at baseline.
source: Using single-cell RNA sequencing, eight distinct endothelial clusters were resolved, including alveolar aerocytes (aCap) ECs expressing apelin at baseline and general capillary (gCap) ECs expressing the apelin receptor.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq gene expression data showing apelin expression in Cluster 2 (aCap ECs) at day 0 (Figure 6A).

claim: General capillary (gCap) ECs express the apelin receptor at baseline.
source: Using single-cell RNA sequencing, eight distinct endothelial clusters were resolved, including alveolar aerocytes (aCap) ECs expressing apelin at baseline and general capillary (gCap) ECs expressing the apelin receptor.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq gene expression data showing Aplnr expression in gCap ECs at day 0 (Figure 6A).

claim: At 3 days post-injury, a novel gCap EC population emerged characterized by de novo expression of apelin.
source: At 3 days post-injury, a novel gCap EC population emerged characterized by de novo expression of apelin, together with the stem cell marker, protein C receptor.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq showing apelin expression in Zone 2 of Cluster 1 at day 3 and immunofluorescence staining (Figures 6A, 6C).

claim: The novel gCap EC population at 3 days post-injury expresses the stem cell marker protein C receptor (Procr).
source: At 3 days post-injury, a novel gCap EC population emerged characterized by de novo expression of apelin, together with the stem cell marker, protein C receptor.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq and immunofluorescence showing co-expression of apelin and PROCR at day 3 (Figures 6A, 6B, 6C).

claim: Stem-like cells transitioned at 5 days to proliferative endothelial progenitor-like cells expressing apelin receptor and Foxm1.
source: These stem-like cells transitioned at 5 days to proliferative endothelial progenitor-like cells, expressing apelin receptor together with the pro-proliferative transcription factor, Foxm1, and were responsible for the rapid replenishment of all depleted EC populations by 7 days post-injury.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq showing Aplnr and Foxm1 expression in Zone 3 of Cluster 1 and Cluster 7 at day 5, along with Mki67 expression (Figures 4C, 6A, 6—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Proliferative endothelial progenitor-like cells were responsible for the rapid replenishment of all depleted EC populations by 7 days post-injury.
source: These stem-like cells transitioned at 5 days to proliferative endothelial progenitor-like cells, expressing apelin receptor together with the pro-proliferative transcription factor, Foxm1, and were responsible for the rapid replenishment of all depleted EC populations by 7 days post-injury.
evidence: Supported by RNA velocity analysis showing vectors from Cluster 1 to other EC clusters, and recovery of EC numbers by day 7 (Figures 1E, 4D, 5A).

claim: Treatment with an apelin receptor antagonist prevented ALI resolution and resulted in excessive mortality.
source: Treatment with an apelin receptor antagonist prevented ALI resolution and resulted in excessive mortality, consistent with a central role for apelin signaling in EC regeneration and microvascular repair.
evidence: Supported by survival data showing all mice treated with ML221 (apelin receptor antagonist) succumbed to DT-induced ALI by 5 days (Figure 10C).

claim: Apelin signaling plays a central role in EC regeneration and microvascular repair.
source: Treatment with an apelin receptor antagonist prevented ALI resolution and resulted in excessive mortality, consistent with a central role for apelin signaling in EC regeneration and microvascular repair.
evidence: Supported by the effect of apelin receptor antagonist on survival and the temporal expression pattern of apelin and its receptor during EC regeneration (Figures 6A, 10C).

claim: ALI and ARDS remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients, accounting for ~30% of ICU admission with 28 day mortality approaching 40%.
source: ALI and its severe clinical counterpart, the adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients, accounting for ~30% of ICU admission with 28 day mortality approaching 40% (Ranieri et al., 2012; Wheeler and Bernard, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Ranieri et al., 2012; Wheeler and Bernard, 2007).

claim: No specific therapies have been developed that improve outcomes in ARDS despite decades of research.
source: Despite decades of research, no specific therapies have been developed that improve outcomes in ARDS (Ranieri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Ranieri et al., 2012).

claim: COVID-19 infection leads to a particularly severe form of ARDS.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the devastating nature of this condition as infection with the SARS CoV2 virus leads to a particularly severe form of ARDS (Fan et al., 2020; Batah and Fabro, 2021) which has been responsible for the vast majority of over 5 million deaths world-wide.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Fan et al., 2020; Batah and Fabro, 2021).

claim: COVID-19-associated ARDS has a strong vascular component characterized by intense endothelial inflammation (endothelialitis) and necrosis.
source: COVID-19-associated ARDS has a strong vascular component which is characterized by intense endothelial inflammation (endothelialitis) and necrosis (Ackermann et al., 2020; Lowenstein and Solomon, 2020; Joffre et al., 2022), consistent with the emerging role of endothelial injury in other forms of ALI leading to the breakdown of the air-blood barrier (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Ackermann et al., 2020; Lowenstein and Solomon, 2020; Joffre et al., 2022).

claim: Endothelial injury plays an emerging role in ALI leading to the breakdown of the air-blood barrier.
source: COVID-19-associated ARDS has a strong vascular component which is characterized by intense endothelial inflammation (endothelialitis) and necrosis (Ackermann et al., 2020; Lowenstein and Solomon, 2020; Joffre et al., 2022), consistent with the emerging role of endothelial injury in other forms of ALI leading to the breakdown of the air-blood barrier (Jin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Jin et al., 2020).

claim: Endothelial repair is required for the resolution of ALI.
source: Indeed, recent reports have suggested that endothelial repair is required for the resolution of ALI (Minamino and Komuro, 2006; Huang et al., 2012), and thus an important target for the development of novel therapeutic strategies.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Minamino and Komuro, 2006; Huang et al., 2012).

claim: Forkhead box M1 (Foxm1) has been implicated as a driver of endothelial cell proliferation and microvascular repair required for ALI resolution.
source: In experimental models the transcription factor, Forkhead box M1 (Foxm1), has been implicated as a driver of endothelial cell (EC) proliferation and microvascular repair that is required for ALI resolution (Huang et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2014; Mirza et al., 2010), and apelin has been reported to protect against inflammation and oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Huang et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2014; Mirza et al., 2010).

claim: Apelin has been reported to protect against inflammation and oxidative stress.
source: In experimental models the transcription factor, Forkhead box M1 (Foxm1), has been implicated as a driver of endothelial cell (EC) proliferation and microvascular repair that is required for ALI resolution (Huang et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2014; Mirza et al., 2010), and apelin has been reported to protect against inflammation and oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Zhang et al., 2018).

claim: During angiogenesis, apelin is induced in endothelial tip cells by tissue hypoxia and VEGF and signals to trailing stalk ECs that express the apelin receptor.
source: During angiogenesis, apelin is induced in endothelial tip cells by tissue hypoxia and VEGF and signals to trailing stalk ECs that express the apelin receptor (Eyries et al., 2008; Kidoya and Takakura, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Eyries et al., 2008; Kidoya and Takakura, 2012).

claim: Apelin plays an important role in vascular development and angiogenesis.
source: Even though apelin is known to play an important role in vascular development and angiogenesis (Kidoya and Takakura, 2012; Yan et al., 2020), the relevance of this peptide for microvascular repair in ALI and ARDS has not been explored.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kidoya and Takakura, 2012; Yan et al., 2020).

claim: The relevance of apelin for microvascular repair in ALI and ARDS has not been explored.
source: Even though apelin is known to play an important role in vascular development and angiogenesis (Kidoya and Takakura, 2012; Yan et al., 2020), the relevance of this peptide for microvascular repair in ALI and ARDS has not been explored.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: ECs play a key role in orchestrating tissue repair through the self-renewal and differentiation of resident stem and progenitor cells in an organ-specific manner.
source: It has increasingly been recognized that ECs play a key role in orchestrating tissue repair through the self-renewal and differentiation of resident stem and progenitor cells in an organ-specific manner (Rafii et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Rafii et al., 2016).

claim: Two specialized lung microvascular EC populations have been described in the normal lung: aerocytes (aCap ECs) characterized by apelin expression, and general (gCap) ECs expressing the apelin receptor.
source: Using this approach, two specialized lungs microvascular EC populations have recently been described in the normal lung Gillich et al., 2020; 'aerocytes' (aCap ECs), which are characterized by the expression of apelin, and general (gCap) ECs expressing the apelin receptor.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Gillich et al., 2020).

claim: Aerocytes are highly differentiated, large cells that make up the endothelial component of the alveolar air-blood barrier and are incapable of proliferation.
source: Aerocytes are highly differentiated, large cells that make up the endothelial component of the alveolar air-blood barrier and are incapable of proliferation (Gillich et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Gillich et al., 2020).

claim: gCap ECs are smaller and located at thicker regions of the alveolar wall.
source: In contrast, gCap ECs are smaller and located at thicker regions of the alveolar wall (Gillich et al., 2020) and respond to injury by proliferation; therefore, represent the lung EC population within which endothelial stem cells may arise.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Gillich et al., 2020).

claim: gCap ECs respond to injury by proliferation.
source: In contrast, gCap ECs are smaller and located at thicker regions of the alveolar wall (Gillich et al., 2020) and respond to injury by proliferation; therefore, represent the lung EC population within which endothelial stem cells may arise.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Gillich et al., 2020).

claim: gCap ECs represent the lung EC population within which endothelial stem cells may arise.
source: In contrast, gCap ECs are smaller and located at thicker regions of the alveolar wall (Gillich et al., 2020) and respond to injury by proliferation; therefore, represent the lung EC population within which endothelial stem cells may arise.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proliferative capacity of gCap ECs and citation to Gillich et al., 2020.

claim: Binary transgenic animals harboring Cdh5-cre-iDTR were obtained by crossing homozygous DTR and Cdh5 mice to generate double heterozygous offspring.
source: Binary transgenic animals harboring Cdh5-cre-iDTR were obtained by crossing homozygous DTR and Cdh5 mice to generate double heterozygous offspring (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by description of breeding strategy and Figure 1A showing the genetic construct.

claim: Administration of DT at doses below 20 ng IT was consistent with survival.
source: Administration of DT at doses below 20 ng IT was consistent with survival (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) resulting in modest increases in right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) that was maximal at 10 ng of DT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DT administration resulted in modest increases in right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) that was maximal at 10 ng of DT.
source: Administration of DT at doses below 20 ng IT was consistent with survival (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) resulting in modest increases in right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) that was maximal at 10 ng of DT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by RVSP measurements in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DTR expression was localized to ECs in Cdh5-DTR animals.
source: DTR expression was localized to ECs in Cdh5-DTR animals (Figure 1B) and widespread apoptosis was seen at 3 days post DT administration (10 ng) in Cdh5-DTR mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining showing co-localization of DTR and CD144 (EC marker) in Figure 1B.

claim: Widespread apoptosis was seen at 3 days post DT administration (10 ng) in Cdh5-DTR mice.
source: DTR expression was localized to ECs in Cdh5-DTR animals (Figure 1B) and widespread apoptosis was seen at 3 days post DT administration (10 ng) in Cdh5-DTR mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by activated caspase-3 staining in Figure 1C.

claim: Full recovery of EC numbers occurred by day 7 post-DT administration.
source: Indeed, DT administration resulted in a ~70% reduction in EC numbers at 3 days by flow cytometry (p<0.001) (Figure 1D and E) with full recovery by day 7 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1E showing EC numbers at day 7 returning to baseline levels.

claim: Lung permeability was increased at 3 days post DT administration, returning to normal by 7 days.
source: Lung permeability was increased (p<0.01) at 3 days post DT administration (Figure 2A and B), again returning to normal by 7 days, with no evidence of increased vascular permeability in other organs (Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Evans blue assay data in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: There was no evidence of increased vascular permeability in other organs after DT administration.
source: Lung permeability was increased (p<0.01) at 3 days post DT administration (Figure 2A and B), again returning to normal by 7 days, with no evidence of increased vascular permeability in other organs (Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Evans blue assay data for liver, spleen, kidney, and brain in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At 3 days post-DT, there was a marked increase in the lung injury score consistent with severe ALI.
source: At 3 days, there was a marked increase in the lung injury score (Figure 2C and D) consistent with severe ALI, and this was associated with the influx of CD11b+Ly6G+ neutrophils by flow cytometry (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis and lung injury scoring in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: The increase in lung injury score at 3 days was associated with the influx of CD11b+Ly6G+ neutrophils.
source: At 3 days, there was a marked increase in the lung injury score (Figure 2C and D) consistent with severe ALI, and this was associated with the influx of CD11b+Ly6G+ neutrophils by flow cytometry (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2E showing increased CD11b+Ly6G+ cells.

claim: Multiplexed scRNA-seq analysis was performed on lung tissues of Cdh5-DTR mice at baseline (day 0) and 3, 5, and 7 days post DT administration.
source: Multiplexed scRNA-seq analysis was performed on lung tissues of Cdh5-DTR mice at baseline (day 0) and 3, 5, and 7 days post DT administration (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental design schematic in Figure 3A.

claim: UMAP dimensionality reduction maps revealed 35 separate cell populations, representing immune, endothelial, stromal, and epithelial cells.
source: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) dimensionality reduction maps of the data revealed 35 separate cell populations, representing immune, endothelial, stromal, and epithelial cells (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by UMAP plots in Figure 3B showing 35 distinct clusters.

claim: Endothelial and monocyte-macrophage populations showed the greatest changes in gene expression profiles after DT administration.
source: Endothelial and monocyte-macrophage populations showed the greatest changes in gene expression profiles after DT administration (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by UMAP plots showing distribution of cells across timepoints in Figure 3C.

claim: Cell types most affected by DT treatment included ECs (Clusters 4, 5, and 0) and macrophages (Clusters 20 and 21).
source: Cell types that were most affected by DT treatment were identified using Augur (Skinnider et al., 2021) and included ECs (Clusters 4, 5, and 0) and macrophages (Clusters 20 and 21) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by Augur analysis results in Figure 3D.

claim: Pericytes and type 2 pneumocytes (Clusters 31 and 8) were among the top 10 cell types most affected by EC ablation.
source: Pericytes and type 2 pneumocytes (Clusters 31 and 8) were also among the top 10 most affected by EC ablation.
evidence: Supported by Augur analysis results in Figure 3D.

claim: Five EC populations exhibited gene expression profiles typical for alveolar gCap ECs (Clusters 0, 1, 3, 6, and 7).
source: We identified eight distinct ECs Clusters (Figure 4A), including five populations that exhibited gene expression profiles typical for alveolar gCap ECs (Clusters 0, 1, 3, 6, and 7) and one that corresponded to aCap ECs (Cluster 2), which are also called aerocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Gillich et al., 2020; Niethamer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citations to Gillich et al., 2020; Niethamer et al., 2020.

claim: One EC population corresponded to aCap ECs (Cluster 2), also called aerocytes.
source: We identified eight distinct ECs Clusters (Figure 4A), including five populations that exhibited gene expression profiles typical for alveolar gCap ECs (Clusters 0, 1, 3, 6, and 7) and one that corresponded to aCap ECs (Cluster 2), which are also called aerocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Gillich et al., 2020; Niethamer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citations to Gillich et al., 2020; Niethamer et al., 2020.

claim: Cluster 1 was made up of 4 distinct 'zones', each zone specific to a single time point before and after EC ablation.
source: Cluster 1 was unique in that it was made up of 4 distinct 'zones'; each zone specific to a single time point before and after EC ablation (Figure 4B), whereas Cluster 7 emerged mainly at 5 days after EC injury and was characterized by a high expression of Mki67, a marker of proliferating cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by UMAP plots in Figure 4B showing temporal distribution of cells within Cluster 1.

claim: Cluster 7 emerged mainly at 5 days after EC injury and was characterized by high expression of Mki67, a marker of proliferating cells.
source: Cluster 1 was unique in that it was made up of 4 distinct 'zones'; each zone specific to a single time point before and after EC ablation (Figure 4B), whereas Cluster 7 emerged mainly at 5 days after EC injury and was characterized by a high expression of Mki67, a marker of proliferating cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by Mki67 expression data in Figure 4C.

claim: Most endothelial populations, including aCap ECs, exhibited a marked decline in cell numbers after DT-induced EC ablation, some reaching a nadir of almost 90% cell loss at 5 days.
source: Most endothelial populations, including aCap ECs, exhibited a marked decline in cell numbers after DT-induced EC ablation, some reaching a nadir of almost 90% cell loss at 5 days (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by cell number quantification in Figure 4D.

claim: Only Clusters 1 and 7 showed stable or increased cell numbers and evidence of EC proliferation.
source: Only Clusters 1 and 7 showed stable or increased cell numbers, and these were the only clusters that showed evidence of EC proliferation, consistent with their role in lung microvascular repair.
evidence: Supported by cell number data in Figure 4D and Mki67 expression in Figure 4C.

claim: Clusters 1 and 7 play a role in lung microvascular repair.
source: Only Clusters 1 and 7 showed stable or increased cell numbers, and these were the only clusters that showed evidence of EC proliferation, consistent with their role in lung microvascular repair.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proliferative capacity and stable cell numbers of these clusters.

claim: RNA velocity analysis revealed strong vectors from Cluster 1 to other EC Clusters that were depleted by EC ablation, including Clusters 0 and 3 (gCap ECs), Cluster 4 (venous), and Cluster 5 (arterial).
source: To explore the role of ECs in Cluster 1 in regenerating microvascular ECs after endothelial injury, we performed RNA velocity and trajectory analysis using scVelo (Python) (Bergen et al., 2020). This revealed strong vectors from Cluster 1 to other EC Clusters that were depleted by EC ablation, including Clusters 0 and 3 (gCap ECs), Cluster 4 (venous), and Cluster 5 (arterial) (Figure 5A), consistent with a central role of this transitional cluster in microvascular regeneration and repair.
evidence: Supported by RNA velocity analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: Cluster 1 plays a central role in microvascular regeneration and repair.
source: To explore the role of ECs in Cluster 1 in regenerating microvascular ECs after endothelial injury, we performed RNA velocity and trajectory analysis using scVelo (Python) (Bergen et al., 2020). This revealed strong vectors from Cluster 1 to other EC Clusters that were depleted by EC ablation, including Clusters 0 and 3 (gCap ECs), Cluster 4 (venous), and Cluster 5 (arterial) (Figure 5A), consistent with a central role of this transitional cluster in microvascular regeneration and repair.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNA velocity analysis showing vectors from Cluster 1 to other EC populations.

claim: Zone 2 of Cluster 1 exhibited evidence of DNA synthesis (S score).
source: This was also supported by evidence of DNA synthesis (S score), localized to Zone 2, and cell proliferation (G2M score) within Zone 3 of Cluster 1 as well as the proliferative Cluster 7 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle scoring analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: Zone 3 of Cluster 1 and Cluster 7 showed cell proliferation (G2M score).
source: This was also supported by evidence of DNA synthesis (S score), localized to Zone 2, and cell proliferation (G2M score) within Zone 3 of Cluster 1 as well as the proliferative Cluster 7 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle scoring analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: Eight genes are associated with the transition from Cluster 1 to Cluster 0.
source: Moreover, we identified the top 15 driver genes implicated in these transitions (Figure 5C), with eight genes associated with the transition from Cluster 1 to Cluster 0, 5 genes involved in the transition of Cluster 1 to aCap ECs (Cluster 2), and 2 genes for Cluster 1 to venous ECs.
evidence: Supported by driver gene analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: Five genes are involved in the transition of Cluster 1 to aCap ECs (Cluster 2).
source: Moreover, we identified the top 15 driver genes implicated in these transitions (Figure 5C), with eight genes associated with the transition from Cluster 1 to Cluster 0, 5 genes involved in the transition of Cluster 1 to aCap ECs (Cluster 2), and 2 genes for Cluster 1 to venous ECs.
evidence: Supported by driver gene analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: Two genes are involved in the transition from Cluster 1 to venous ECs.
source: Moreover, we identified the top 15 driver genes implicated in these transitions (Figure 5C), with eight genes associated with the transition from Cluster 1 to Cluster 0, 5 genes involved in the transition of Cluster 1 to aCap ECs (Cluster 2), and 2 genes for Cluster 1 to venous ECs.
evidence: Supported by driver gene analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: An inferred latent time plot of the 300 top driver genes revealed temporal progression of gene expression originating with Cluster 1, progressing through Cluster 0, and terminating in Cluster 2.
source: Finally, an inferred latent time plot of the 300 top driver genes revealed the same temporal progression of gene expression as observed with the independent timepoint analysis (Figure 5D). This originated with Cluster 1, progressed through Cluster 0, and terminated in Cluster 2 at the end of the pseudotime cascade.
evidence: Supported by latent time analysis in Figure 5D.

claim: At baseline (day 0), apelin was uniquely expressed in aCap ECs of Cluster 2.
source: At baseline (day 0), apelin was found to be uniquely expressed in aCap ECs of Cluster 2 (Figure 6A) as previously reported (Gillich et al., 2020; Vila Ellis et al., 2020), whereas apelin receptor (Aplnr) was found only in gCap ECs.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figure 6A and citations to Gillich et al., 2020; Vila Ellis et al., 2020.

claim: At baseline (day 0), apelin receptor (Aplnr) was found only in gCap ECs.
source: At baseline (day 0), apelin was found to be uniquely expressed in aCap ECs of Cluster 2 (Figure 6A) as previously reported (Gillich et al., 2020; Vila Ellis et al., 2020), whereas apelin receptor (Aplnr) was found only in gCap ECs.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figure 6A.

claim: aCap ECs exhibit predominant expression of EC tip cell genes including Kdr (Vegfr2), Npl1 (neuropilin 1), and Cd34.
source: In addition to apelin, aCap ECs also exhibited predominant expression of other EC tip cell genes including Kdr (Vegfr2), Npl1 (neuropilin 1), and Cd34 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Blanco and Gerhardt, 2013; Zecchin et al., 2017), whereas stalk cell markers, such as Hey1, Flit1, and Notch1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) was mainly expressed by gCap ECs.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and citations to Blanco and Gerhardt, 2013; Zecchin et al., 2017.

claim: Stalk cell markers, such as Hey1, Flit1, and Notch1, are mainly expressed by gCap ECs.
source: In addition to apelin, aCap ECs also exhibited predominant expression of other EC tip cell genes including Kdr (Vegfr2), Npl1 (neuropilin 1), and Cd34 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Blanco and Gerhardt, 2013; Zecchin et al., 2017), whereas stalk cell markers, such as Hey1, Flit1, and Notch1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) was mainly expressed by gCap ECs.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The gCap EC population in Zone 2 of Cluster 1 at 3 days post-injury robustly expressed gCap markers, with the exception of Aplnr.
source: Three days after EC injury, de novo expression of apelin was seen in the newly emergent gCap EC population in Zone 2 of Cluster 1 (Figure 6A). This population robustly expressed gCap markers, with the exception of Aplnr (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figures 4 and 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The gCap EC population in Zone 2 of Cluster 1 exhibited expression of Procr (protein C receptor or EPCR), a marker of bipotent resident vascular endothelial stem cells.
source: Interestingly, they also exhibited the expression of Procr (protein C receptor or EPCR; Figure 6A), a marker of bipotent resident vascular endothelial stem cells (Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figure 6A and citation to Yu et al., 2016.

claim: Co-expression of apelin with Procr and Cd93 was evident at 3 days post-injury.
source: Co-expression of apelin with Procr, as well as Cd93 (a gCap marker) was evident at 3 days post-injury (Figure 6B) and confirmed by immunofluorescence staining (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by two-gene analysis in Figure 6B and immunofluorescence in Figure 6C.

claim: This represents the first demonstration of apelin expression by gCap ECs.
source: To our knowledge, this represents the first demonstration of apelin expression by gCap ECs.
evidence: This is a statement about novelty of the finding.

claim: Angpt2 (angiopoietin 2) was uniquely expressed in the endothelial stem cell-like population at 3 days post-injury.
source: As well, Angpt2 (angiopoietin 2) (Maisonpierre et al., 1997) was uniquely expressed in this endothelial stem cell-like population (Maisonpierre et al., 1997), together with the progenitor cell marker, Cd34 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and citation to Maisonpierre et al., 1997.

claim: The progenitor cell marker Cd34 was expressed in the endothelial stem cell-like population at 3 days post-injury.
source: As well, Angpt2 (angiopoietin 2) (Maisonpierre et al., 1997) was uniquely expressed in this endothelial stem cell-like population (Maisonpierre et al., 1997), together with the progenitor cell marker, Cd34 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 5 days post-DT, new populations emerged in Zone 3 of Cluster 1 and in Cluster 7 exhibiting expression of Mki67, Aplnr, and Foxm1.
source: At day 5 post-DT, new populations emerged in Zone 3 of Cluster 1, as well as in Cluster 7 (Figure 4B) exhibiting expression of Mki67, a marker of cell proliferation, together with the Aplnr (Figure 6A) and Foxm1, a pro-proliferative transcription factor (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B); however, the density of proliferating cells was greatest in Cluster 7.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figures 4B, 6A, and 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The density of proliferating cells was greatest in Cluster 7 at day 5 post-DT.
source: At day 5 post-DT, new populations emerged in Zone 3 of Cluster 1, as well as in Cluster 7 (Figure 4B) exhibiting expression of Mki67, a marker of cell proliferation, together with the Aplnr (Figure 6A) and Foxm1, a pro-proliferative transcription factor (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B); however, the density of proliferating cells was greatest in Cluster 7.
evidence: Supported by visual inspection of Mki67 expression density in Figure 4C.

claim: By day 7, the expression of PROCR/EPCR was nearly entirely lost.
source: By day 7, the expression of PROCR/EPCR was nearly entirely lost (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining in Figure 6C showing absence of EPCR at day 7.

claim: By day 7, apelin expression was restored to baseline profile, being restricted to aCap ECs (aerocytes).
source: This was consistent with a restoration of the baseline profile of apelin expression being restricted to aCap ECs (aerocytes).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figure 6A showing apelin expression pattern at day 7 similar to day 0.

claim: The proliferative Cluster 7 showed the greatest increase in transcription factor activity, with Foxm1 being among the top candidates.
source: Not surprisingly, the greatest increase in TF activity was seen in the proliferative Cluster 7, with Foxm1 being among the top candidates.
evidence: Supported by decoupleR transcription factor analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Other transcription factors involved in cell cycle regulation were identified in Cluster 7, including three members of the E2f family, Myc, and Tfdp1.
source: Other TFs known to be involved in cell cycle regulation were also identified, including three members of the E2f family, Myc, and Tfdp1.
evidence: Supported by decoupleR transcription factor analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Strong Nanog and Sox10 activity, which play important roles in stem cells and developmental biology, was unique to aCap ECs.
source: As well, strong Nanog and Sox10 activity, which play important roles in stem cells and developmental biology, was unique to aCap ECs.

claim: In an LPS-induced ALI model, a gCap EC cluster co-expressing Apln/Procr was apparent as early as 6 hr post-LPS.
source: At baseline (day 0), apelin was only expressed by the aCap ECs, and Procr was not expressed at all (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D). After LPS-induced injury, a gCap EC cluster co-expressing Apln/Procr was apparent as early as 6 hr post-LPS, followed by the emergence of a proliferative Mki67/Foxm1-postive population at day 3.
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of publicly available scRNA-seq data (GSE148499) shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3D.

claim: In an LPS-induced ALI model, a proliferative Mki67/Foxm1-positive population emerged at day 3.

claim: Analysis of a publicly available atlas of the aging lung revealed a significant reduction in lung apelin expression in mice with age.
source: An analysis of a publicly available atlas of the aging lung (Angelidis et al., 2019) revealed a significant reduction in lung apelin expression in mice (Figure 10A) which was confirmed in the Cdh5-DTR double transgenic mice by RT-qPCR (Figure 10B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of published data (Angelidis et al., 2019) shown in Figure 10A and RT-qPCR data in Figure 10B.

claim: Aging reduced survival post-DT-induced injury with only 24% of 52-week-old Cdh5-DTR mice surviving to day 7 post-DT compared to 82% survival for 12-week-old mice.
source: Interestingly, aging reduced survival post-DT-induced injury with only 24% of 52-week-old Cdh5-DTR mice surviving to day 7 post-DT compared to 82% survival for 12-week-old mice (p<0.01) (Figure 10C).
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 10C.

claim: When young Cdh5-DTR mice were treated with an apelin receptor antagonist (ML221), all mice succumbed to DT-induced acute lung injury by 5 days.
source: Moreover, when young Cdh5-DTR mice were treated with an apelin receptor antagonist, ML221, all mice succumbed to DT-induced acute lung injury by 5 days (Figure 10C), consistent with a failure of lung microvascular repair.
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 10C.

claim: Selective ablation of lung ECs results in severe ALI with many features of ARDS seen in various clinical contexts, including COVID-19.
source: We have established that selective ablation of lung ECs results in severe ALI with many features of ARDS seen in various clinic contexts, including COVID-19.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The loss of more than 70% of lung ECs was compatible with survival by virtue of an efficient endogenous regenerative response that resulted in near complete restoration of the lung microvascular structure and function in just one week.
source: Remarkably, the loss of more than 70% of lung ECs was compatible with survival by virtue of an efficient endogenous regenerative response that resulted in near complete restoration of the lung microvascular structure and function in just one week.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings showing EC depletion and recovery.

claim: This model underscores the importance of the endothelium in the pathogenesis of ALI.
source: This model underscores the importance of the endothelium in the pathogenesis of ALI and affords a unique opportunity to explore the mechanisms underlying EC regeneration and microvascular repair, which is critical for ALI resolution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that EC ablation alone is sufficient to cause severe ALI.

claim: Apelin-positive, gCap ECs showed no evidence of proliferation at 3 days post-injury.
source: Apelin-positive, gCap ECs showed no evidence of proliferation at 3 days post-injury; however, by 5 days they transitioned to a highly proliferative phenotype with expression of apelin being replaced by its receptor, consistent with a dynamic role for the apelinergic system in driving a transition from the endothelial tip- to stalk-like, proliferative progenitor cells (Palm et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by Mki67 expression data showing absence of proliferation in Zone 2 at day 3 (Figure 4C).

claim: By 5 days, apelin-positive gCap ECs transitioned to a highly proliferative phenotype with expression of apelin being replaced by its receptor.
source: Apelin-positive, gCap ECs showed no evidence of proliferation at 3 days post-injury; however, by 5 days they transitioned to a highly proliferative phenotype with expression of apelin being replaced by its receptor, consistent with a dynamic role for the apelinergic system in driving a transition from the endothelial tip- to stalk-like, proliferative progenitor cells (Palm et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data showing Aplnr and Mki67 expression in Zone 3 at day 5 (Figures 4C, 6A).

claim: The apelinergic system plays a dynamic role in driving a transition from endothelial tip- to stalk-like, proliferative progenitor cells.
source: Apelin-positive, gCap ECs showed no evidence of proliferation at 3 days post-injury; however, by 5 days they transitioned to a highly proliferative phenotype with expression of apelin being replaced by its receptor, consistent with a dynamic role for the apelinergic system in driving a transition from the endothelial tip- to stalk-like, proliferative progenitor cells (Palm et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal expression pattern of apelin and its receptor, supported by citation to Palm et al., 2016.

claim: Procr has been suggested to be a marker of primitive, endothelial-like hematopoietic precursors (i.e. pre-HSCs) that give rise to both ECs and HSCs during development.
source: Speculation and Ideas: Procr has been suggested to be a marker of primitive, endothelial-like hematopoietic precursors (i.e. pre-HSCs) (Lan, 2017) that give rise to both ECs and HSCs during development (Dzierzak and Bigas, 2018), playing a critical role in the early genesis of both blood and blood vessels.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Lan, 2017; Dzierzak and Bigas, 2018).

claim: Procr has been reported to be expressed by ~90% of bone marrow side population cells, which are thought to have important regenerative activity.
source: Procr has also been reported to be expressed by ~90% of bone marrow side population cells (Balazs et al., 2006), which are thought to have important regenerative activity.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Balazs et al., 2006).

claim: Procr was not expressed by any EC population in the healthy lung, and only appeared transiently in the gCap endothelial stem- and progenitor-like cells during microvascular repair.
source: However, Procr was not expressed by any EC population in the healthy lung, and only appeared transiently in the gCap endothelial stem- and progenitor-like cells during the microvascular repair.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data in Figure 6A showing Procr expression only at day 3.

claim: Lung vascular injury results in a re-activation of a fundamental vascular stem cell that is central to both vascular development and repair.
source: This suggests that lung vascular injury results in a re-activation of a fundamental vascular stem cell that is central to both vascular development and repair.
evidence: This is speculation based on the transient expression of Procr during repair.

claim: On day 3 post-DT-induced ablation, ~15% of all lung ECs expressed Procr.
source: Indeed, on day 3 post-DT-induced ablation, ~15% of all lung ECs expressed Procr making their isolation feasible using commercially available kits for PROCR.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the scRNA-seq data.

claim: The lung has a remarkable capacity for microvasculature EC regeneration which is orchestrated by newly emergent apelin-expressing gCap endothelial stem-like cells.
source: The lung has a remarkable capacity for microvasculature EC regeneration which is orchestrated by newly emergent apelin-expressing gCap endothelial stem-like cells that give rise to highly proliferative, apelin receptor-positive endothelial progenitors responsible for the regeneration of the lung microvasculature.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on all the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: Apelin-expressing gCap endothelial stem-like cells give rise to highly proliferative, apelin receptor-positive endothelial progenitors responsible for the regeneration of the lung microvasculature.
source: The lung has a remarkable capacity for microvasculature EC regeneration which is orchestrated by newly emergent apelin-expressing gCap endothelial stem-like cells that give rise to highly proliferative, apelin receptor-positive endothelial progenitors responsible for the regeneration of the lung microvasculature.
